extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, especially epistemology and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the conditions and limits of human cognition: what constitutes knowledge, why knowledge is necessarily relative, and whether anything unconditioned (the Absolute) can be known. Discusses implications for consciousness, classification, and the role of life/intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational nature of subject and object
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject exists only as it is related to the object; the object exists only insofar as it is apprehended by a subject; destruction of either is the destruction of consciousness itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies the claim that being conscious of the Absolute (an object independent of relation) is self-contradictory: to know the Absolute as such would require treating it both as related and unrelated to consciousness, which is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge requires comparison and mutual consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To know that an object given in relation to our consciousness is identical with one existing independently, we must be able to compare the two; such comparison is itself an act of consciousness and requires consciousness of both objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore we cannot be conscious of the Absolute as identical with an object existing 'out of relation to consciousness' because that would demand comparing a conscious and a non-conscious object; the comparison makes the supposed non-conscious object part of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognition involves the triad: relation, difference, likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every complete act of consciousness, besides distinction and relation, also implies likeness; a thought involves relation, difference, and likeness, and whatever does not present each of these does not admit of cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification and recognition (assimilation of impressions to prior states) are necessary for orderly consciousness. Without assimilation (likeness) cognition would be chaos; thus cognition presupposes both differentiation and integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition/assimilation is necessary for knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a mental state can become an idea it must be known as separate from prior states and as of the same kind with certain other previous states; new impressions are known to the extent they are assimilated to previously seen objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains how cognition arises gradually (infant development example) and why novel objects are known only insofar as they can be assimilated/classified with prior experience; absolute novelty resists full cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification requirement for knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing is perfectly known only when it is in all respects like certain previously observed things; in proportion to the respects in which it is unlike them is the extent to which it is unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence anything that cannot be classed with other things (i.e., absolutely unshared attributes) is beyond the bounds of knowledge. The Unconditioned, classable neither with the conditioned nor with any other unconditioned, cannot be classed at all and so is unknowable by this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unconditioned/Absolute is 'trebly unthinkable'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because thought involves relation, difference, and likeness, the Unconditioned (which presents none of these) is unthinkable in three ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal argument supports the doctrine of the relativity of knowledge: what lacks relation, difference, and likeness cannot be cognized by thought as we know it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life and intelligence as continuous adjustment of internal to external relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is definable as the continuous adjustment of internal relations to external relations; intelligence shows itself when external relations to which internal ones are adjusted become numerous, complex, and remote in time or space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this biological/functional perspective we see why knowledge is necessarily relative: cognition and intelligence are systems of correlating internal states with external relations (co-existences and sequences), so knowledge can only capture relations, not things-in-themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical knowledge requires correspondence of relations not identity
rubrics_metrics.description: For practical guidance it suffices that subjective relations (a and b) uniformly correspond to objective properties (x and p); it matters nothing if internal states are like external properties in themselves, only that their relations correspond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if x uniformly accompanies p externally, and a uniformly accompanies b internally, then recognition of a triggers expectation of b and appropriate action; knowledge useful for life is about these correspondences, not metaphysical identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative/conceptual negation of the Absolute is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that the Absolute is conceived merely by a negation of conceivability or as the mere absence of conditions under which consciousness is possible is not strictly true; such formulations omit an all-important indefinite positive consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author critiques Hamilton and Mansel: the very act of reasoning that the Absolute is unknowable presupposes a positive (though vague) notion of the Absolute. The 'negation-only' account cannot account for the nascent, positive element present in our thought of the Unconditioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlatives imply a residuary positive consciousness of the correlative
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraries (e.g., Limited/Unlimited, Relative/Non-relative) are conceived as correlatives; the abstraction of limits leaves a residuary consciousness of something which filled their outlines, and this constitutes our positive, indefinite consciousness of the Non-relative or Absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore thinking of the Relative already invokes an indefinite positive awareness of the Absolute; if the Absolute were only pure negation, the relation between Relative and Non-relative would be unthinkable and thought itself would collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of conception produce nascent awareness of the unbounded
rubrics_metrics.description: When we imagine a bounded space/time/cause, a simultaneous nascent consciousness of space/time/cause beyond the bound arises; this nascent consciousness is positive though unshaped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Momentum of thought carries us beyond conditioned existence to unconditioned existence; such nascent, indefinite consciousness is like the conscious elements that suggest it, and persists as an unformable yet positive element of thought.
